title: SPECIAL REPORT: Inside AI scam ads exploiting TikTok’s advertising system to defraud Nigerians

reading.body:
This is a case of impersonation carried out through a platform's paid advertising system. The ads used deepfake video and cloned voices to present themselves as banks, telecoms firms and public figures, and they were distributed as promotions rather than as organic posts. The failure sits at the point where an advertiser buys placement: the content passed through TikTok's ad system and reached users, and the money moved after victims submitted details or transferred funds.

The techniques involved are established by the reporting: synthetic likenesses of real brands and people, ads in multiple languages including Pidgin, Yoruba and Hausa, comments disabled, no AI labels, and advertiser details that could not be traced. Catching this would have required verification of who was buying the ads and moderation that worked in the languages the ads were written in. The reporter's archive of 130 ads over five weeks, with OPay impersonated in 28, indicates the pattern was repeated and visible rather than a single slip.

What is not established is what TikTok or Nigerian regulators will do in response, and the reporting does not attribute intent to any party. The victim losses described are individual accounts, and the figures for national scam losses come from the article's cited estimate rather than from an adjudicated finding.

reports.title: SPECIAL REPORT: Inside AI scam ads exploiting TikTok’s advertising system to defraud Nigerians

summary:
A Premium Times investigation found that AI-generated scam ads are running as paid promotions on TikTok and defrauding Nigerians. The ads use deepfake videos and cloned voices to impersonate brands such as OPay, UBA, MTN and Airtel, plus public figures like Aliko Dangote and the Emir of Kano. One victim, Mohammed Yusuf, lost about N150,000 after submitting his details to a fake OPay ad. Another, Ahmad Wura, lost roughly N1 million in cryptocurrency. The reporter archived 130 such ads over five weeks, with OPay impersonated in 28 of them.

The ads promise grants, loans, giveaways and investment returns, and they appear in English, Pidgin, Yoruba and Hausa. Many had comments disabled, no AI labels and untraceable advertiser details. Experts blame weak advertiser verification and gaps in moderating local-language content. The article says Nigeria loses over $500 million yearly to scams, and it calls for stronger digital governance, but it does not state what TikTok or regulators will do next.
